extracted.intended_audience: researchers of peer review and scholarly-publishing policy makers (journal editors, scientometrics scholars, research administrators)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and designing incentive schemes (monetary and non-monetary) for scholarly peer review, weighing effects on reviewer effort, fairness, scalability, and the public-good nature of peer review. Focuses on empirical findings and policy/implementation constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary incentives displace social ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetary incentives can crowd out social/non-monetary motivations for tasks like peer review — i.e., offering money can reduce the effectiveness of existing social drivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim supported by prior literature (Heyman & Ariely, Psychological Science, 2004). Slide summary: 'Monetary incentives displace social ones.' Implication: introducing payments may undermine reputation, duty, or altruistic motivations that sustain peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of payment level on reviewer effort (no/low/medium)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different payment levels produce different effort outcomes: low levels of payment can produce lower effort than no payment, while medium levels may produce effort similar to the no-payment case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From experimental evidence (Heyman & Ariely): trivial task with no/low/medium payment — 'Effort for low levels of payment is lower than in the no-payment case'; 'Effort for medium levels of payment is just as in the no-payment case.' Design implication: payment magnitude matters nonlinearly and small payments can be counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-monetary incentives do not lead to crowding-out
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-monetary (social/material) incentives tend not to cause crowding-out effects and therefore are less likely to undermine intrinsic/social motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarized from Heyman & Ariely: 'Non-monetary incentives do not lead to crowding-out effects.' Suggests preference for non-monetary recognition, reputation signals, or institutional rewards over cash pay in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low or generic monetary incentives reduce fairness in review
rubrics_metrics.description: In experiments simulating review processes, low, generic monetary incentives led to lower fairness than offering no incentives at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical result reported from Squazzoni et al., Research Policy, 2013: 'Low, generic incentives led to lower fairness than no incentives at all.' Indicates that poorly designed or blunt monetary rewards can worsen evaluative quality or equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carefully aligned incentives required to preserve fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Only carefully-aligned monetary incentives can achieve a level of fairness comparable to the no-incentive situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From experimental findings: 'Only carefully aligned incentives allow to reach a level of fairness close to the no-incentive situation.' Implication: incentive schemes must be tailored to reviewer motivations and task specifics to avoid harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization transforms peer review into a market context
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing monetary incentives changes the social context of peer review by creating market-like dynamics, where reviewer behavior and the quality of reviews depend on wage-like payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slide question/observation: 'The presence of monetary incentives changes the context of peer review to a "market" situation; Where the quality of the work depends on the wage level!' Policy implication: consider how marketization affects norms, expectations, and reviewer selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration challenge: matching incentives to effort
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical difficulty is calibrating monetary incentives to elicit the desired level of referee effort across heterogeneous reviewers and tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slide raises: 'how is it possible to carefully calibrate the incentive to the referee’s effort?' Design implication: calibration requires understanding variability in reviewer costs, tasks, and responses — a nontrivial measurement and administrative problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability and funding feasibility of paying reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Scaling up monetary incentives to pay millions of referees annually faces major feasibility questions: how to offer high incentives at scale and who will fund them (e.g., taxpayers, publishers)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slide queries: 'how is it possible to offer high incentives to millions of referees every year? who should pay for that? the taxpayers?' Consider budgetary, equity, and incentive-compatibility constraints when proposing payment schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-journal displacement effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetary incentives offered by some journals may 'displace' existing social incentives in other journals, producing system-wide externalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slide asks: 'will monetary incentives offered by some journals "displace" social incentives in others?' Indicates need to evaluate field-level and inter-journal effects, not only per-journal policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review is a common/public-good; markets are inefficient providers
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review exhibits common/public-good characteristics, and pure market mechanisms are an inefficient way to provide such public goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slide conclusions: 'Peer review holds common/public-good characters' and 'Market as an inefficient provider of public goods.' Suggests favoring collective, institutional, or community-based solutions over marketization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional and social arrangements can manage the commons
rubrics_metrics.description: Commons literature indicates that management through institutional and social arrangements (e.g., community governance, norms, reputation systems) can successfully sustain peer-review as a public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slide conclusion: 'Commons literature: management through institutional and social arrangements works.' Recommend designing institutions (editoral policies, recognition systems) that bolster trust and cooperative norms rather than relying on cash payments alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust and reputation mechanisms are key governance tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Trust and reputation mechanisms, when enhanced by well-designed institutions, can support high-quality peer review without monetary payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slide: 'Working of trust and reputation mechanisms enhanced by carefully designed institutions.' Practical implication: build transparent recognition, credit, and accountability systems to incentivize effort and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary incentives can displace material incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetary incentives can replace or undermine existing material incentives (e.g., modest perks) and change incentive structures in unintended ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slide bullet: 'Material incentives displaced by monetary ones.' Design implication: consider interactions between different incentive types; introducing cash may alter the meaning/effect of prior non-cash rewards.
